extracted.intended_audience: general practitioners, medical students, and informed lay readers
extracted.subtask_short: clinical description and treatment of infectious diseases
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-style clinical overviews of common infectious diseases (typhoid, mumps, whooping cough, erysipelas, malaria), covering development/incubation, symptoms, complications, prognosis, detection, treatment, nursing care, and prevention. Aimed to guide diagnosis, home care, and public-health precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — fever pattern and stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive, sustained fever with characteristic daily pattern over weeks: high and about the same each evening, falling one or two degrees in the morning; third week gradual fall in evening high; fourth week may be subnormal in morning and a degree above normal at night; fever may be prolonged five to six weeks in some cases; relapses occur in ~10% of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature course described by week: first week rising, second week often delirium, third week improvement in moderate cases, fourth week falling to normal in favorable cases. Continued very high fever (105–106°F) is an unfavorable sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — early symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Prodromal lassitude and disinclination for exertion; disease begins with headache, backache, loss of appetite, sometimes chill (adults) or convulsion (children), muscle soreness, abdominal pain, occasional nosebleed, vomiting or diarrhea, coated/cracked tongue, cough, flushed face, pulse ~100 increasing thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are common to many acute diseases; gradual onset with constant fever, nosebleed, and loose bowels are most suggestive of typhoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — rose spots as diagnostic sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Pin-head–sized pink-red spots on chest and belly appearing at end of first week or ten days, two or three up to many, that disappear on pressure and return immediately; appear in crops during second and third weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When present (especially with the described course) they make the existence of typhoid fever 'pretty certain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — mental and neurological manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: During second week delirium and nocturnal wandering; stupor with dusky flushed face; brownish, cracked tongue; third-week severe cases show stupor, muttering delirium, twitching of wrists, picking at bedclothes, trembling with movement, slow hesitant speech, emaciation, urinary and fecal incontinence; patient may appear insane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May require watching to prevent self-injury; these signs mark severity and complication risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — pulse rate as severity indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulse ranges from 80–120/minute in typical cases; severe cases show rapid feeble pulse 120–140/minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rising pulse with weakness indicates worsening and higher risk of severe outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — unfavorable prognostic signs and acute complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfavorable signs: continued very high fever (105–106°F), marked delirium, early muscle trembling, and bleeding from bowels. Acute life-threatening complications include pneumonia, perforation and hemorrhage from the bowel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intense sudden abdominal pain with vomiting suggests intestinal perforation — an emergency. Bleeding occurs in 4–6% of cases and accounts for ~15% of deaths; perforation in 1–2% accounts for ~10% of deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — detection and differential diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Laymen cannot determine typhoid absolutely; physician often cannot be sure before end of first week or ten days; examination of the blood offers an exact method of diagnosis. Typhoid with chills may be mistaken for malaria in malarial regions, but true coinfection is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blood examination after ~1 week to confirm; consider regional disease patterns (malaria) in differential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — complications and long-term sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: Complications: diarrhea, delirium, mental and nervous diseases, bronchitis, pleurisy, pneumonia, ear abscess, bowel perforation and hemorrhage, gall bladder inflammation, disease of heart/kidney/bladder, others. Sequels: boils, baldness, bone disease, painful spine, less commonly insanity and consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convalescence may take weeks to months; organ damage and systemic sequels can persist despite recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — overall treatment philosophy (Rest, Diet, Bathing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Essentials of treatment are rest (absolute quiet, horizontal), diet (chiefly liquids until a week after fever disappears), and bathing (cold water/sponging to reduce temperature and relieve delirium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physician care strongly desirable, but in remote settings outcomes may not be greatly altered; mainstay is supportive nursing and infection control rather than a specific curative medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — nursing care and handling of discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute quiet in horizontal position from first suspicion; assist to turn in bed; patient must not rise; urine and bowel discharges collected in bedpan or urinal under cover; for bowel bleeding receive discharges in cloths without stirring patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pressure or movement that could precipitate bleeding/perforation; prevent contagion via careful disposal and attendant hygiene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — dietary regimen and refeeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquid diet until one week after fever resolution: diluted milk chief food; albumen water (raw egg white diluted and flavored), raw beef juice, coffee, cocoa, strained gruels, broths, custard, jellies, ice cream, milk-and-flour porridge, eggnog; finely scraped raw/rare beef, soft toast, soft-boiled/poached eggs allowable after first week of normal temperature; solid foods withheld until 2–3 weeks after fever departs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a cup of liquid every two hours except during some sleeping hours; abundant water; avoid coarse/uncooked vegetables and fruit when resuming solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — bathing and external temperature control
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cold water to lower temperature and relieve restlessness/delirium when temperature >102.5°F; methods include sponging with ice water, enveloping body in sheet wet at ~65°F with rubbing and ice, or vapor bath (cheese cloth wetted at 100–105°F then sprinkled with ~98°F water and fanned) for children who object to cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubbing chest/sides during cold applications prevents shock; use cold cloth on head and hot-water bottle at feet; repeat every 2–3 hours if needed; dry gently and avoid agitating feeble patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — symptomatic medicines and surgical/nuisance care
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicines generally not required except for special symptoms. Brandy or whisky diluted may be valuable in severe cases with muttering delirium, dry tongue, feeble pulse (tablespoonful every 2–4 hours). Diarrhea >4/day: bismuth subnitrate 1/4 tsp or paregoric 1 tsp every 3 hours. Constipation: warm soapsuds injections every 2 days. Bleeding: perfect quiet, oral ice lumps, reduce nourishment; 15 drops laudanum for adult restlessness; whiskey if pulse feeble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve stimulants until needed; use local pads (flannel wrung from hot water with turpentine) for abdominal pain; white of egg/water and beef juice may help distention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — prevention and disinfection procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict disposal and disinfection of excreta and contaminated materials: bowel discharges submerged in milk of lime (1:4 water) for one hour before emptying; urine mixed with equal carbolic solution (1:20) and left one hour; clothing/linen soaked in carbolic solution two hours; expectoration on muslin burned; bedpans and eating utensils scalded; attendants wash hands after contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no water-closet, bury disinfected discharges at least 100 feet from any well or stream. Typhoid derived from germs escaping in urine and bowel/nose/mouth discharges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumps — definition and affected structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagious disease characterized by inflammation of parotid glands (below and in front of ears), sometimes other salivary glands, and rarely testicles in males and breasts in females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swelling from injury or as complication of other diseases is distinct from epidemic mumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumps — incubation and communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Incubation period 1–3 weeks after exposure. The germ has not been discovered (in this text) and exact means of communication are unknown; breath suspected; patient can communicate disease for ten days after fever has passed and should be isolated for that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High attack rates in susceptible young persons; one attack usually protects against another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumps — characteristic symptoms and course
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins with pain and swelling below the ear, unilateral then often bilateral within 48 hours; swelling firm, sensitive, tightness making chewing/swallowing difficult; fever ~101°F (rarely 103–104°F) for 4–5 days; swelling peaks 2–5 days then subsides and disappears within 10–14 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earache and noises frequent; difficulty in speech and refusal of food common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumps — complications and sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: Common complication in post-pubertal males is painful, swollen testicles during recovery or 1–2 weeks later; may cause cessation of testicular development though sexual vigor usually retained. Less often breasts and female sexual organs affected; rare abscess/gangrene of parotid, meningitis, nervous and joint complications, recurring or permanent swelling and hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most cases recover without mishap except testicular involvement risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumps — treatment and symptomatic care
rubrics_metrics.description: Bed rest during fever, liquid diet, tepid sponging for fever, ice cap on head for high fever/delirium; pain relief by hot compress (sheet cotton wrung out of hot water, covered with oil-silk) to neck; paregoric dosing (tablespoon adult; teaspoon child 8–10) diluted and spaced; testicular inflammation: bed rest, elevation, hot compresses, suspensory bandage, and daily ointment (guiacol 60 grains, lard 1/2 ounce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of paregoric and topical measures described; get supportive care and monitor complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping cough — contagion, epidemiology, and age distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagious disease with fits of coughing and a characteristic whoop; transmitted by direct contact with sick (rarely via room or objects). Occurs chiefly in children 6 months to 6 years, often epidemic and following measles outbreaks; one attack usually confers immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Girls and weak/delicate children slightly more susceptible; some children are naturally immune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping cough — incubation/development period
rubrics_metrics.description: Variable incubation 2 days to 2 weeks, usually 7–10 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prodrome like an ordinary head cold precedes the characteristic cough phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping cough — characteristic cough pattern and clinical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Coughing fits worsen (worse at night) culminating after days to weeks in episodes of 15–20 short coughs without breath culminating in a long crowing whoop, facial congestion/blueing, eyeball protrusion, venous prominence, sometimes vomiting and large expectoration; number of fits variable (mild 6–12/day; severe 40–80/day); attacks last seconds to 1–2 minutes; disease duration usually 3–6 weeks but may last months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whoop may be absent in some cases; fits are provoked by emotion, crying, singing, eating, drinking, temperature change, and bad air. Contagiousness usually ~2 months or until cough ceases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping cough — complications and severe outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Complications: bronchitis, pneumonia (especially in winter), diarrhea (in summer), convulsions in infants, nosebleed and petechiae from raised venous pressure, severe vomiting, pleurisy, permanent heart damage, lung rupture, paralysis from intracranial hemorrhage. Majority of children over 2 recover without dangerous sequels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly critical in infants under two and weak children; seek physician care when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping cough — treatment strategy and recommended medicines
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresh air and strict isolation; keep children in bed if severe; vaporize antiseptics in room (2% carbolic acid or vapo-cresoline); atomized resorcin or hydrogen dioxide solutions for throat. Early: paregoric + syrup of ipecac; daytime: bromide of sodium; nighttime: chloral for sleep; tincture of belladonna daytime; quinine dosing by age; bromoform in severe cases. Suggested sequence when no physician: belladonna daytime + bromide sodium at night; if fails after 5 days use bromide + chloral; severe cases use bromoform. Supportive: hold/support head during fits; slap with wet towel if breathing ceases; cod-liver oil in convalescence; change of air helps later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dosages given by age in text; most drugs should be used with medical advice. Emphasize environment (fresh air, ventilation) and gradual nutritional support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erysipelas — cause and modes of spread
rubrics_metrics.description: Caused by germs entering through wounds or abrasions of skin or mucous membranes; contagious in the sense that germs may be carried by nurses, furniture, bedding, dressings, clothing, etc.; not transmitted at a distance through air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern surgical cleanliness has reduced hospital/childbirth forms; sometimes arises without visible wound, usually on face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erysipelas — characteristic clinical signs and course
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins with severe chill or convulsion in babies and fever, vomiting, headache, lassitude; a sharply demarcated red patch appears (face common) spreading like a drop of oil; skin tense, smooth, shiny, scarlet, swollen, often with small blisters; pain, burning or itching and great tension; temperature may reach 104°F; subsides in ~4–5 days with scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borders well marked; on face swelling may close eye and interfere with breathing; relapse common but usually milder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erysipelas — complications, systemic involvement, and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Spreading may produce deep abscesses, tissue destruction; internal organs (heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys) occasionally involved with serious consequences; higher mortality in old, diseased, alcoholic, and newborn. Rarely, erysipelas may be followed by cure of malignant growths or chronic ulcers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity varies; hospital vs private practice mortality differences noted in data elsewhere in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erysipelas — treatment and infection control
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolate patient in well-ventilated, sunlit room; burn or boil dressings and contaminated objects; liquid diet; apply cloths wet with cold water or solutions (½ tsp pure carbolic acid per pint hot water or sugar of lead 4 grains per pint) over inflamed areas; reduce fever by frequent full-body sponging with cold water; tablespoon whisky or brandy in water every 2 hours if pulse weak; painting borders with contractile collodion may prevent spread; quarantine until scaling ceases (usually two weeks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some topical solutions (sugar of lead) are toxic; follow recommended precautions; emphasize quarantine and disinfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaria — definition and transmission via Anopheles mosquito
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaria is due to a minute animal parasite which inhabits the body of mosquitoes and is transmitted to humans by bites of infected Anopheles mosquitoes; not contagious by direct contact between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two essentials for malaria in a region: presence of the particular mosquito and infection of that mosquito with the malarial parasite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaria — environmental causes and mosquito ecology
rubrics_metrics.description: Mosquito life and malaria transmission require moisture and suitable temperature (average not less than 60°F); damp soil, marshes, or bodies of water favor malaria. Seasonality: common in temperate climates in summer/autumn, less in spring and rare in winter; in tropics/subtropics present year-round but more in spring/fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refutes older 'miasma' ideas; factors that favor mosquitoes (not 'night air' per se) explain patterns of disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaria — mosquito identification (Anopheles vs Culex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anopheles (host of malarial parasite) usually has mottled wings and rests on wall with body at ~45° angle and hind legs hanging down; Culex (common house mosquito) holds body parallel to wall, wings usually not mottled, hind legs carried up over back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful field morphological clues to distinguish vectors in domestic settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaria — parasite life cycle and relation to fever periodicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parasite enters and develops within human red blood cells, multiplies by dividing; chills and fever occur at the stage when parasites divide. Different parasite types have different development times (common form 48 hours causing attacks every other day; some forms every third day). When multiple parasite groups exist, attacks may occur daily or at irregular intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual reproduction of parasite occurs in mosquito (not human); variability in synchrony of parasite development explains irregular fever patterns in severe forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaria — distribution and regional severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaria widely distributed: more severe in tropics and warmer temperate regions. In US, present in parts of New England (Connecticut Valley), near Boston, around Philadelphia, New York, Baltimore (less frequent and milder), and more severe along Gulf and Mississippi valleys (Mississippi, Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas), though less widespread than formerly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional prevalence and form severity vary historically and geographically; consider local epidemiology in assessment.
